title: Delete
summary: Delete a key in each of the three cases and draw the resulting tree.

hook.goal: Delete a key from a BST in each of the three cases (leaf, one child, two children) and describe the resulting tree.

scenario.title: Removing a contact
scenario.text: You delete a contact. The search from Lesson 2 must still find everyone else.
scenario.recall: What could go wrong when you take a node out of the middle of the tree?

cases.label: Remove 70 from T

Move 80 up and hang 60 under it

cases.note: That keeps the rule here, but only because 60 and 80 are leaves. If they had their own children, one of them would have nowhere to go. The lesson shows a method that always works.

explore.prompt: Which removal was hardest, and why?

options.text: Removing 70: it had two children, so it was not obvious what should replace it
options.reply: Most students say so. Case 3 needs a rule, the in-order successor, which you will see next.

options.text: Removing 40: its child had to move up
options.reply: Moving a single child up is case 2. The two-children case needs a rule; you will see it next.
A leaf is the easy case. The two-children case needs a rule; you will see it next.

pages.title: Three cases
steps: Step 0: find the node with search.
Case 2, one child: replace the node with its child. The child's whole subtree moves up.
Case 3, two children: find the in-order successor, the minimum of the right subtree.
Copy the successor's key into the node.
Then delete the successor's old node from the right subtree. It has at most one child, so this is case 1 or 2.
Why it works: the successor is larger than every key on the left and smaller than every other key on the right, so the BST rule still holds.
pages.note: The mirror option uses the predecessor, the maximum of the left subtree. This app uses the successor.
pages.caption: 20 is a leaf, so deleting it is case 1. 70 has two children, so deleting it is case 3; its successor is 80.

steps.right: Two children, 60 and 80, so this is case 3.

steps.prompt: Click the in-order successor of 70: the smallest key in its right subtree.
steps.right: 80. Go right to 80, then left as far as you can; 80 has no left child.
steps.wrong: Start in 70's right subtree (outlined), then go left as far as you can.

steps.right: Copy 80 into the node that held 70.
steps.wrong: Case 3 always uses the successor you just found.

steps.prompt: What happens to the old 80 node?
options: Remove it: it is a leaf (case 1)
steps.right: Done. 80 now has left child 60, and the in-order sequence is still sorted.
steps.wrong: The old 80 is now a duplicate. It must go.

items.prompt: After any delete, is the in-order sequence still sorted?

hints.text: A correct delete keeps the BST rule. What does the BST rule guarantee about in-order?
In-order dots are shown on the tree. Read them from left to right.

items.explanation: Yes. A correct delete keeps the BST rule, and the BST rule makes in-order sorted.
